claim: Increased mTORC1 signaling from TSC1/TSC2 inactivation is found in cancer.
source: Increased mTORC1 signaling from TSC1/TSC2 inactivation is found in cancer and causes tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about TSC1/TSC2 inactivation.

claim: Increased mTORC1 signaling from TSC1/TSC2 inactivation causes tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).
source: Increased mTORC1 signaling from TSC1/TSC2 inactivation is found in cancer and causes tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about TSC1/TSC2 inactivation.

claim: Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had shortened lifespans.
source: Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had shortened lifespans and extensive hamartomas containing abnormal tortuous, dilated vessels prominent in the forelimbs.
evidence: Supported by survival analysis data presented in Figure 1F showing median survival of approximately 24 weeks.

claim: Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had extensive hamartomas containing abnormal tortuous, dilated vessels prominent in the forelimbs.
source: Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had shortened lifespans and extensive hamartomas containing abnormal tortuous, dilated vessels prominent in the forelimbs.
evidence: Supported by histological and imaging data presented in Figure 2 and related figures.

claim: Abnormalities in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice were blocked by the mTORC1 inhibitor sirolimus.
source: Abnormalities were blocked by the mTORC1 inhibitor sirolimus.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing reduction in tumor size and dermal thickness with sirolimus treatment.

claim: A Tsc2/mTORC1 expression signature identified in Tsc2-deficient fibroblasts was increased in bladder cancers with TSC1/TSC2 mutations in the TCGA database.
source: A Tsc2/mTORC1 expression signature identified in Tsc2-deficient fibroblasts was also increased in bladder cancers with TSC1/TSC2 mutations in the TCGA database.
evidence: Supported by analysis of TCGA data presented in Figure 4E showing higher signature scores in TSC1/TSC2 mutant tumors.

claim: Lgals3 encoding galectin-3 was increased in Tsc2-deficient cells.
source: Signature component Lgals3 encoding galectin-3 was increased in Tsc2-deficient cells and serum of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 4D and protein data in Figure 5.

claim: Lgals3 encoding galectin-3 was increased in serum of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice.
source: Signature component Lgals3 encoding galectin-3 was increased in Tsc2-deficient cells and serum of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 5E showing 67% higher Gal-3 levels in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice.

claim: Galectin-3 was increased in TSC-related skin tumors.
source: Galectin-3 was increased in TSC-related skin tumors, angiomyolipomas, and lymphangioleiomyomatosis with serum levels in patients with lymphangioleiomyomatosis correlating with impaired lung function and angiomyolipoma presence.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and ELISA data in Figure 6.

claim: Galectin-3 was increased in angiomyolipomas.
source: Galectin-3 was increased in TSC-related skin tumors, angiomyolipomas, and lymphangioleiomyomatosis with serum levels in patients with lymphangioleiomyomatosis correlating with impaired lung function and angiomyolipoma presence.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6F.

claim: Galectin-3 was increased in lymphangioleiomyomatosis.
source: Galectin-3 was increased in TSC-related skin tumors, angiomyolipomas, and lymphangioleiomyomatosis with serum levels in patients with lymphangioleiomyomatosis correlating with impaired lung function and angiomyolipoma presence.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6E.

claim: Serum galectin-3 levels in patients with lymphangioleiomyomatosis correlate with impaired lung function.
source: Galectin-3 was increased in TSC-related skin tumors, angiomyolipomas, and lymphangioleiomyomatosis with serum levels in patients with lymphangioleiomyomatosis correlating with impaired lung function and angiomyolipoma presence.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis in Figure 6G showing negative correlation between %FEV1 and Gal-3 levels.

claim: Serum galectin-3 levels in patients with lymphangioleiomyomatosis correlate with angiomyolipoma presence.
source: Galectin-3 was increased in TSC-related skin tumors, angiomyolipomas, and lymphangioleiomyomatosis with serum levels in patients with lymphangioleiomyomatosis correlating with impaired lung function and angiomyolipoma presence.
evidence: Supported by analysis in Figure 6H showing higher Gal-3 levels in mild LAM patients with AML.

claim: mTORC1 is a central regulator of cell growth and metabolism.
source: Mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) is a central regulator of cell growth and metabolism (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Laplante and Sabatini, 2012.

claim: Activation of mTORC1 caused by dysregulated upstream signaling through phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), PTEN, AKT, and TSC1-TSC2 is observed in cancers.
source: Activation of mTORC1, caused by dysregulated upstream signaling through phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), PTEN, AKT, and TSC1-TSC2, is observed in cancers, hamartoma syndromes such as tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), and vascular anomalies (Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Krymskaya and Goncharova, 2009; Nathan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Krymskaya and Goncharova, 2009; Nathan et al., 2017.

claim: Activation of mTORC1 caused by dysregulated upstream signaling is observed in hamartoma syndromes such as tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC).
source: Activation of mTORC1, caused by dysregulated upstream signaling through phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), PTEN, AKT, and TSC1-TSC2, is observed in cancers, hamartoma syndromes such as tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), and vascular anomalies (Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Krymskaya and Goncharova, 2009; Nathan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Krymskaya and Goncharova, 2009; Nathan et al., 2017.

claim: Activation of mTORC1 caused by dysregulated upstream signaling is observed in vascular anomalies.
source: Activation of mTORC1, caused by dysregulated upstream signaling through phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), PTEN, AKT, and TSC1-TSC2, is observed in cancers, hamartoma syndromes such as tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), and vascular anomalies (Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Krymskaya and Goncharova, 2009; Nathan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Krymskaya and Goncharova, 2009; Nathan et al., 2017.

claim: Many pathological abnormalities in conditions with mTORC1 activation arise from increased signaling through mTORC1.
source: The supposition that many of the pathological abnormalities in these conditions arise from increased signaling through mTORC1 is supported by response to treatment using mTOR inhibitors such as sirolimus and everolimus, particularly for tumors in TSC (Bissler et al., 2008; Krueger et al., 2010; McCormack et al., 2011; Taveira-DaSilva et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing clinical response to mTOR inhibitors.

claim: Clinical responses to mTOR inhibitors may be inadequate and require lifelong treatment.
source: However, clinical responses may be inadequate and require lifelong treatment (Taveira-DaSilva and Moss, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Taveira-DaSilva and Moss, 2015.

claim: Facial angiofibromas can be disfiguring.
source: Facial angiofibromas can be disfiguring and their highly vascular nature makes them prone to bleeding with minimal trauma (Darling et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Darling et al., 2010.

claim: Facial angiofibromas are prone to bleeding with minimal trauma due to their highly vascular nature.
source: Facial angiofibromas can be disfiguring and their highly vascular nature makes them prone to bleeding with minimal trauma (Darling et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Darling et al., 2010.

claim: Angiomyolipomas (AMLs) are a leading cause of death in patients with TSC due to hemorrhage and renal failure.
source: Angiomyolipomas (AMLs) are a leading cause of death in patients with TSC due to hemorrhage and renal failure (Franz et al., 2010; Byard et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Franz et al., 2010; Byard et al., 2003.

claim: Angiomyolipomas have large, tortuous, and thick-walled vessels that may lack elastin.
source: They have large, tortuous, and thick-walled vessels that may lack elastin, making them prone to aneurysms and life-threatening hemorrhage (Byard et al., 2003; Bissler and Kingswood, 2004; Tweeddale et al., 1955).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Byard et al., 2003; Bissler and Kingswood, 2004; Tweeddale et al., 1955.

claim: Angiomyolipoma vessels are prone to aneurysms and life-threatening hemorrhage.
source: They have large, tortuous, and thick-walled vessels that may lack elastin, making them prone to aneurysms and life-threatening hemorrhage (Byard et al., 2003; Bissler and Kingswood, 2004; Tweeddale et al., 1955).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Byard et al., 2003; Bissler and Kingswood, 2004; Tweeddale et al., 1955.

claim: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) involves a proliferation of abnormal smooth-muscle like cells that invade the axial lymphatics and lung.
source: Lymphangioleiomyomatosis (LAM) involves a proliferation of abnormal smooth-muscle like cells that invade the axial lymphatics and lung to cause lymphangioleiomyomas and cystic lung disease, respectively (Taveira-DaSilva and Moss, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Taveira-DaSilva and Moss, 2015.

claim: Sporadic LAM (S-LAM) is associated with the development of AMLs.
source: LAM occurring in the absence of TSC, called sporadic LAM (S-LAM), is also associated with the development of AMLs (Taveira-DaSilva and Moss, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Taveira-DaSilva and Moss, 2015.

claim: VEGF-D is elevated in LAM.
source: The lymphangiogenic factor VEGF-D is elevated in LAM, correlates with disease severity and response to treatment, and is associated with lymphatic involvement (McCormack et al., 2011; Glasgow et al., 2009; Young et al., 2013; Seyama et al., 2006; Budde et al., 2016; Malinowska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: VEGF-D correlates with disease severity in LAM.
source: The lymphangiogenic factor VEGF-D is elevated in LAM, correlates with disease severity and response to treatment, and is associated with lymphatic involvement (McCormack et al., 2011; Glasgow et al., 2009; Young et al., 2013; Seyama et al., 2006; Budde et al., 2016; Malinowska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: VEGF-D correlates with response to treatment in LAM.
source: The lymphangiogenic factor VEGF-D is elevated in LAM, correlates with disease severity and response to treatment, and is associated with lymphatic involvement (McCormack et al., 2011; Glasgow et al., 2009; Young et al., 2013; Seyama et al., 2006; Budde et al., 2016; Malinowska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: VEGF-D is associated with lymphatic involvement in LAM.
source: The lymphangiogenic factor VEGF-D is elevated in LAM, correlates with disease severity and response to treatment, and is associated with lymphatic involvement (McCormack et al., 2011; Glasgow et al., 2009; Young et al., 2013; Seyama et al., 2006; Budde et al., 2016; Malinowska et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: VEGF-D is increased in a mouse model of LAM.
source: VEGF-D is also increased in a mouse model of LAM (Goncharova et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Goncharova et al., 2012.

claim: TSC and S-LAM are caused by inactivating mutations in either TSC1 or TSC2.
source: TSC and S-LAM are caused by inactivating mutations in either TSC1 or TSC2 (Cheadle et al., 2000), genes that are also mutated in some cancers, particularly bladder carcinoma (Sjödahl et al., 2011; Pymar et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cheadle et al., 2000 and others.

claim: TSC1 and TSC2 are mutated in some cancers, particularly bladder carcinoma.
source: TSC and S-LAM are caused by inactivating mutations in either TSC1 or TSC2 (Cheadle et al., 2000), genes that are also mutated in some cancers, particularly bladder carcinoma (Sjödahl et al., 2011; Pymar et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sjödahl et al., 2011; Pymar et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2013.

claim: TSC1 and TSC2 proteins suppress mTORC1 signaling by forming a ternary complex with TBC1D7.
source: Proteins encoded by the TSC1 and TSC2 genes, TSC1 (also known as hamartin) and TSC2 (aka tuberin), suppress mTORC1 signaling by forming a ternary complex with TBC1D7 that suppresses RHEB-mediated activation of signaling through mTORC1 by converting RHEB-GTP to RHEB-GDP (Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Dibble et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Dibble et al., 2012.

claim: The TSC1-TSC2-TBC1D7 complex suppresses RHEB-mediated activation of mTORC1 by converting RHEB-GTP to RHEB-GDP.
source: Proteins encoded by the TSC1 and TSC2 genes, TSC1 (also known as hamartin) and TSC2 (aka tuberin), suppress mTORC1 signaling by forming a ternary complex with TBC1D7 that suppresses RHEB-mediated activation of signaling through mTORC1 by converting RHEB-GTP to RHEB-GDP (Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Dibble et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dibble and Cantley, 2015; Dibble et al., 2012.

claim: Loss of function of either TSC1 or TSC2 inhibits RHEB inactivation, leading to hyperactive mTORC1 signaling.
source: Loss of function of either TSC1 or TSC2 inhibits RHEB inactivation, leading to hyperactive mTORC1 signaling (Dibble et al., 2012; Huang and Manning, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dibble et al., 2012; Huang and Manning, 2008.

claim: mTORC1 incorporates signals from growth factor signaling, especially through the PI3K-AKT pathway.
source: mTORC1 incorporates signals from growth factor signaling, especially through the PI3K-AKT pathway, and acts as a sensor of cellular stress, levels of amino acids, energy, and oxygen to mediate its downstream effects (Dibble and Cantley, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dibble and Cantley, 2015.

claim: mTORC1 acts as a sensor of cellular stress, levels of amino acids, energy, and oxygen.
source: mTORC1 incorporates signals from growth factor signaling, especially through the PI3K-AKT pathway, and acts as a sensor of cellular stress, levels of amino acids, energy, and oxygen to mediate its downstream effects (Dibble and Cantley, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dibble and Cantley, 2015.

claim: In the Eker rat, renal tumors develop with 100% penetrance.
source: In the Eker rat, renal tumors develop with 100% penetrance and these rats additionally develop pituitary adenomas, uterine leiomyomas, and splenic tumors (Eker, 1954; Yeung et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eker, 1954; Yeung et al., 1994.

claim: Eker rats develop pituitary adenomas, uterine leiomyomas, and splenic tumors.
source: In the Eker rat, renal tumors develop with 100% penetrance and these rats additionally develop pituitary adenomas, uterine leiomyomas, and splenic tumors (Eker, 1954; Yeung et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Eker, 1954; Yeung et al., 1994.

claim: Homozygous disruption of Tsc1 or Tsc2 is lethal during embryogenesis in mice.
source: In mice, homozygous disruption of Tsc1 or Tsc2 is lethal during embryogenesis, and heterozygous Tsc1+/− and Tsc2+/− mice develop renal cystadenomas, liver hemangiomas, and infrequently, paw angiosarcomas (Kobayashi et al., 1999; Onda et al., 1999; Kobayashi et al., 2001; Kwiatkowski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 1999; Onda et al., 1999; Kobayashi et al., 2001; Kwiatkowski et al., 2002.

claim: Heterozygous Tsc1+/− and Tsc2+/− mice develop renal cystadenomas, liver hemangiomas, and infrequently, paw angiosarcomas.
source: In mice, homozygous disruption of Tsc1 or Tsc2 is lethal during embryogenesis, and heterozygous Tsc1+/− and Tsc2+/− mice develop renal cystadenomas, liver hemangiomas, and infrequently, paw angiosarcomas (Kobayashi et al., 1999; Onda et al., 1999; Kobayashi et al., 2001; Kwiatkowski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kobayashi et al., 1999; Onda et al., 1999; Kobayashi et al., 2001; Kwiatkowski et al., 2002.

claim: Conditional disruption of Tsc1 in vascular smooth muscle cells resulted in mice with vascular smooth muscle hyperplasia and hypertension.
source: Conditional disruption of Tsc1 in vascular smooth muscle cells resulted in mice with vascular smooth muscle hyperplasia and hypertension (Malhowski et al., 2011; Houssaini et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Malhowski et al., 2011; Houssaini et al., 2016.

claim: Deletion of Tsc1 expression specifically in endothelial cells using Tie2-cre led to embryonic lethality with embryos displaying a disorganized vascular network with edema and hemorrhage.
source: Deletion of Tsc1 expression specifically in endothelial cells using Tie2-cre led to embryonic lethality with embryos displaying a disorganized vascular network with edema and hemorrhage (Ma et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2014.

claim: Using an inducible Tie2-cre to disrupt Tsc1 in postnatal mice resulted in cutaneous lymphangiosarcomas and Prox1-positive thin-walled vascular channels with an increase in VEGFA levels within cutaneous tumors.
source: By using an inducible Tie2-cre to disrupt Tsc1 in postnatal mice, cutaneous lymphangiosarcomas and Prox1-positive thin-walled vascular channels developed with an increase in VEGFA levels within cutaneous tumors (Sun et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sun et al., 2015.

claim: A model of Tsc1 conditional disruption using Darpp32-cre developed kidney cysts by 8 weeks of age and angiosarcomas within the digits visible by postnatal day 21.
source: Another model of Tsc1 conditional disruption using Darpp32-cre developed kidney cysts by 8 weeks of age and angiosarcomas within the digits visible by postnatal day 21 (Leech et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Leech et al., 2015.

claim: TSC skin lesions usually contain TSC2-deficient fibroblast-like cells with hyperactive mTORC1 signaling.
source: Our previous research has demonstrated that TSC skin lesions usually contain TSC2-deficient fibroblast-like cells with hyperactive mTORC1 signaling (Li et al., 2005, 2008; Tyburczy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2005, 2008; Tyburczy et al., 2014.

claim: TSC2-deficient fibroblast-like cells, upon incorporation into xenografts, resulted in skin with increased blood vessel size and number.
source: These fibroblast-like cells, upon incorporation into xenografts, resulted in skin with increased blood vessel size and number (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Dermal but not epidermal TSC2 loss occurs in human TSC skin samples.
source: As we previously determined that dermal but not epidermal TSC2 loss occurs in human TSC skin samples (Li et al., 2008), we hypothesized that conditional disruption of mouse Tsc2 in mesenchymal cells including dermal cells of the skin would be sufficient to induce highly vascular skin tumor formation and produce a source of Tsc2-deficient cells that could be used to discover factors that contribute to TSC tumorigenesis or have potential as diagnostic or prognostic markers of disease.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2008.

claim: Prrx1-cre is regionally expressed within adipocytes, chondrocytes, and osteoblasts, but not blood cells or endothelial cells.
source: In addition to its activity in dermal fibroblasts within these regions, Prrx1-cre is regionally expressed within adipocytes, chondrocytes, and osteoblasts, but not blood cells or endothelial cells (Logan et al., 2002; Greenbaum et al., 2013; Calo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Logan et al., 2002; Greenbaum et al., 2013; Calo et al., 2010.

claim: Mice containing homozygous Tsc2fl allele and heterozygous Prrx1-cre transgene were born live and in expected ratios from crosses.
source: Mice containing homozygous Tsc2fl allele and heterozygous Prrx1-cre transgene (herein, Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice) were born live and in expected ratios from crosses (see Materials and methods section).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from breeding experiments.

claim: EYFP expression was detected in the limbs, ventral skin and craniofacial regions of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice.
source: EYFP expression was detected in the limbs, ventral skin and craniofacial regions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nearly all limb skin fibroblasts contained the recombined Tsc2fl allele.
source: Analysis by PCR showed that nearly all limb skin fibroblasts, but not epidermal cells, contained the recombined Tsc2fl allele (herein, Tsc2- allele) (Figure 1B), confirming mesenchymal specificity.
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Epidermal cells did not contain the recombined Tsc2fl allele.
source: Analysis by PCR showed that nearly all limb skin fibroblasts, but not epidermal cells, contained the recombined Tsc2fl allele (herein, Tsc2- allele) (Figure 1B), confirming mesenchymal specificity.
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Fibroblasts from ventral and limb skin of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice showed nearly undetectable Tsc2 protein.
source: Western blot analysis of fibroblasts from ventral and limb skin of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice (KO) showed nearly undetectable Tsc2 protein in KO as well as increased phosphorylation of S6, indicating mTORC1 hyperactivation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Fibroblasts from Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice showed increased phosphorylation of S6, indicating mTORC1 hyperactivation.
source: Western blot analysis of fibroblasts from ventral and limb skin of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice (KO) showed nearly undetectable Tsc2 protein in KO as well as increased phosphorylation of S6, indicating mTORC1 hyperactivation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Approximately 95% of cultured KO neonatal leg skin fibroblasts expressed EYFP.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of cultured KO neonatal leg skin fibroblasts indicated that approximately 95% of cells expressed EYFP (Figure 1D), corresponding to the dramatically reduced level of Tsc2 protein observed in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Postnatal Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had shorter and thicker extremities.
source: Postnatal Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had shorter and thicker extremities, thicker bones of the cranium and limbs and a bulbous snout (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Postnatal Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had thicker bones of the cranium and limbs.
source: Postnatal Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had shorter and thicker extremities, thicker bones of the cranium and limbs and a bulbous snout (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Postnatal Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had a bulbous snout.
source: Postnatal Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had shorter and thicker extremities, thicker bones of the cranium and limbs and a bulbous snout (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dorsal forepaw and whisker pad skin from adult Tsc2cKO mice revealed a thickened, hypercellular dermis.
source: Histological examination of dorsal forepaw (Figure 1E and Figure 1—source data 1) and whisker pad skin (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b) from adult Tsc2cKO mice revealed a thickened, hypercellular dermis.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The median survival of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice was approximately 24 weeks.
source: Survival was reduced in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice with median survival of approximately 24 weeks, and no significant gender difference (Figure 1F and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: There was no significant gender difference in survival of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice.
source: Survival was reduced in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice with median survival of approximately 24 weeks, and no significant gender difference (Figure 1F and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Blood counts and serum chemistry of 17 week old Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice revealed evidence of anemia.
source: Blood counts and serum chemistry were performed on 17 week old Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice to explain early death and revealed evidence of anemia, however serum markers of kidney and liver function were not different from controls (Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by blood count and serum chemistry data in Figure 1—source data 3.

claim: Serum markers of kidney and liver function in 17 week old Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice were not different from controls.
source: Blood counts and serum chemistry were performed on 17 week old Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice to explain early death and revealed evidence of anemia, however serum markers of kidney and liver function were not different from controls (Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by serum chemistry data in Figure 1—source data 3.

claim: A growth on the volar surface of forepaws of all Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice was visible beginning at about 3 weeks of age.
source: A growth on the volar surface of forepaws of all Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice was visible beginning at about 3 weeks of age (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by photographic data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Serial MRI analysis showed fluid-filled spaces and nodular masses in some kidneys as early as 4 weeks and in kidneys of 6 of 6 mice by 12 weeks.
source: Serial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) analysis, done at 4, 8 and 12 weeks of age in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice (n = 6) and controls (WT) of similar age, showed fluid-filled spaces and nodular masses in some kidneys as early as 4 weeks and in kidneys of 6 of 6 mice by 12 weeks (Table 1, Figure 2B green arrow).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: The spleen became enlarged with poorly defined internal structure/patterning in 3 of 6 mice by 8 weeks, and 5 of 6 mice by 12 weeks.
source: The spleen became enlarged with poorly defined internal structure/patterning in 3 of 6 mice by 8 weeks, and 5 of 6 mice by 12 weeks (Table 1 and Figure 2B, blue arrow).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: A fluid-containing abnormality in the subcutaneous layer appeared in the shoulder region near the neck and axilla, which increased in size and frequency with age to become nearly universal by 12 weeks of age.
source: A fluid-containing abnormality in the subcutaneous layer appeared in the shoulder region near the neck and axilla, which increased in size and frequency with age to become nearly universal by 12 weeks of age (Table 1 and Figure 2B, pink arrows).
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Changes in the liver were less frequently detected by MRI, with dark speckling observed in 1/6 animals by 12 weeks of age.
source: Changes in the liver were less frequently detected by MRI, with dark speckling observed in 1/6 animals by 12 weeks of age.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data described in the text and Table 1.

claim: Kidneys of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice showed grossly visible cystic lesions that were microscopically apparent in 9 of 11 mice.
source: Kidneys showed grossly visible cystic lesions (Figure 2C) that were microscopically apparent in 9 of 11 mice.
evidence: This is supported by gross pathology and histological data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: EYFP expression was observed in cyst wall epithelial cells of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice.
source: EYFP expression, an indication of KO cells, was observed in cyst wall epithelial cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Livers of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice developed vascular growths in 8 of 11 mice.
source: Livers developed vascular growths in 8 of 11 Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice (Figure 2C), and contained EYFP expression in vessel intima (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by gross pathology and histological data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Liver vascular growths in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice contained EYFP expression in vessel intima.
source: Livers developed vascular growths in 8 of 11 Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice (Figure 2C), and contained EYFP expression in vessel intima (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: All adult Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice developed enlarged spleens with grossly visible tumor nodules.
source: All adult Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice developed enlarged spleens with grossly visible tumor nodules (Figure 2D, left).
evidence: This is supported by gross pathology data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Histological examination of upper forelimbs showed vascular anomalies with tortuous, dilated blood and lymphatic vessels amid abnormal adipose tissue and skeletal muscle.
source: Histological examination of upper forelimbs showed vascular anomalies with tortuous, dilated blood and lymphatic vessels amid abnormal adipose tissue and skeletal muscle (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Large, dilated vessels in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice contained thin, fragmented elastic fibers reminiscent of those observed in human AML.
source: Large, dilated vessels, many with thick walls, contained thin, fragmented elastic fibers reminiscent of those observed in human AML (Figure 2Eii, Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2Eii and Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Adipose tissue was reduced in the subcutaneous space of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice.
source: Adipose tissue was reduced in the subcutaneous space of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from histological examination.

claim: Hamartomas found in shoulder of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice frequently contained abundant adipose tissue containing plump nuclei, increased cytoplasm, and either single or multiple fat vesicles.
source: In contrast, hamartomas found in shoulder frequently contained abundant adipose tissue containing plump nuclei, increased cytoplasm, and either single or multiple fat vesicles (Figure 2Eiii).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2Eiii.

claim: Abnormal lymphatics in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice contained tortuous lymph node sinuses and vessels lined with plump endothelial cells and surrounded by increased collagen.
source: Abnormal lymphatics contained tortuous lymph node sinuses and vessels lined with plump endothelial cells and surrounded by increased collagen (Figure 2Eiv).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2Eiv.

claim: Abnormal lymphatic vessels in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice expressed typical lymphatic markers (VEGFR3, LYVE1).
source: Abnormal lymphatic vessels expressed typical lymphatic markers (VEGFR3, LYVE1), and also expressed EYFP indicating loss of Tsc2 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Abnormal lymphatic vessels in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice expressed EYFP indicating loss of Tsc2 expression.
source: Abnormal lymphatic vessels expressed typical lymphatic markers (VEGFR3, LYVE1), and also expressed EYFP indicating loss of Tsc2 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: EYFP expression was found throughout the hamartomatous tumors of upper forelimbs and frequently seen in vessels including endothelial cells.
source: EYFP expression was found throughout the hamartomatous tumors of upper forelimbs and frequently seen in vessels including endothelial cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Control vessels from the upper forelimbs showed EYFP expression in connective tissue fibroblasts and mural cells of vessels, but EYFP staining was not observed in luminal cells.
source: In contrast, control vessels from the upper forelimbs showed EYFP expression in connective tissue fibroblasts and mural cells of vessels, but EYFP staining was not observed in luminal cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Within thickened vessels, CD31 staining highlighted abnormal plump endothelial cells and slit-like spaces in the vessel walls.
source: Within thickened vessels, staining using the blood vessel endothelial marker CD31 highlighted abnormal plump endothelial cells and slit-like spaces in the vessel walls (Figure 2H), features not evident in control vessels (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Abnormal vessel walls in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice contained greater numbers of smooth muscle cells in disorganized arrangement than control vessels.
source: These abnormal vessel walls contained greater numbers of smooth muscle cells in disorganized arrangement (Figure 2J) than control vessels from the upper forelimb (Figure 2K).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2J and 2K.

claim: Hamartomas in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice expressed HMB-45 in the anomalous vessels of upper forelimbs.
source: Hamartomas also expressed HMB-45, an immunohistochemical marker of LAM and AMLs, in the anomalous vessels of upper forelimbs (Figure 2L) but not control vessels (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2L.

claim: Control vessels did not express HMB-45.
source: Hamartomas also expressed HMB-45, an immunohistochemical marker of LAM and AMLs, in the anomalous vessels of upper forelimbs (Figure 2L) but not control vessels (Figure 2M).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2M.

claim: Fluid collected from subcutaneous axillary masses outside the thorax contained higher triglyceride than paired serum samples, suggesting a contribution of chylous fluid.
source: This fluid was pink and cloudy (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and contained higher triglyceride than paired serum samples from these mice, suggesting a contribution of chylous fluid (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical analysis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Low levels of Tsc2- allele were present in kidney, liver and spleen of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre neonates, indicating the presence of KO cells before tumor formation.
source: Compared to the expected recombination in the limbs, low levels of Tsc2- allele were present in kidney, liver and spleen of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre neonates, indicating the presence of KO cells before tumor formation (Figure 3A upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3A upper panel.

claim: Tumors of adult Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice showed increased Tsc2- allele, providing evidence of an expansion of KO cells in tumor-containing tissues.
source: Tumors of adult mice showed increased Tsc2- allele, providing evidence of an expansion of KO cells in tumor-containing tissues (Figure 3A, lower panel).
evidence: This is supported by PCR data shown in Figure 3A lower panel.

claim: EYFP-positive cells from Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre spleens had approximately 10% of the Tsc2 exon 3 copy number as cells from WT spleen.
source: EYFP-positive cells had approximately 10% of the Tsc2 exon 3 copy number as cells from WT spleen.
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR copy number assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both Tsc2 exon 6 and Tsc1 copy number were unchanged in EYFP-positive cells from Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre spleens.
source: Both Tsc2 exon 6 (outside of the conditional region) and Tsc1 copy number were unchanged in EYFP-positive cells.
evidence: This is supported by real-time PCR copy number assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: About half of cultured splenocytes from Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice stain for CD90.2, including most EYFP expressing (KO) cells.
source: By flow cytometry, we found that about half of cultured splenocytes stain for CD90.2, including most EYFP expressing (KO) cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cultured cells from dissociated paw tumors contained an endothelial fraction that expressed EYFP.
source: Consistent with IHC results, cultured cells from dissociated paw tumors contained an endothelial fraction that expressed EYFP (Figure 3D, middle right).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Very few EYFP-positive endothelial cells were observed in cells isolated from control EYFP-expressing forepaws.
source: However, in cells isolated from control EYFP-expressing forepaws, we observed very few EYFP-positive endothelial cells (Figure 3D, lower right).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Sirolimus treatment resulted in a significant decrease in forepaw thickness in both male and female Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: In both male and female Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice, a significant decrease in thickness across the middle of the forepaw was observed as compared to forepaws from vehicle-treated mice (Figure 3E and F and Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by measurement data shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: Dermal thickness of the forepaws was reduced 35% in sirolimus-treated Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice compared to vehicle-treated controls.
source: Dermal thickness of the forepaws was reduced 35% compared to vehicle-treated controls (Figure 3G and H and Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by histological measurement data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Forepaw vascular hamartomas were present in 8 of 8 vehicle-treated Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice compared to 1 of 10 sirolimus-treated mice.
source: Post-treatment analysis revealed forepaw vascular hamartomas in 8 of 8 vehicle-treated Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice compared to 1 of 10 sirolimus-treated mice.
evidence: This is stated as a result of post-treatment analysis and supported by data in Table 3.

claim: Kidney tumors and spleen tumors in Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice responded to sirolimus treatment.
source: Kidney tumors and spleen tumors also responded to sirolimus treatment (Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 3.

claim: 1387 genes were overexpressed in KO compared to WT neonatal mouse leg skin fibroblasts.
source: In untreated cells, 1387 genes were overexpressed in KO compared to WT, while 437 were overexpressed in WT compared to KO (false discovery rate <10%).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: 437 genes were overexpressed in WT compared to KO neonatal mouse leg skin fibroblasts.
source: In untreated cells, 1387 genes were overexpressed in KO compared to WT, while 437 were overexpressed in WT compared to KO (false discovery rate <10%).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: The signature in KO fibroblasts included genes involved in glucose metabolism, the regulation of cell cycle, and HIF1α responses.
source: Gene ontology enrichment analysis (see Materials and methods section) revealed that the signature in KO included genes involved in glucose metabolism, the regulation of cell cycle, and HIF1α responses.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis of RNA sequencing data.

claim: Sirolimus treatment resulted in 7282 underexpressed genes in KO fibroblasts and 2567 overexpressed genes in KO fibroblasts.
source: To confirm that elevated mTORC1 signaling had an expected role in Tsc2-deficient KO fibroblasts, KO and WT neonatal dermal fibroblasts were treated with 20 nM sirolimus for 24 hr. Sirolimus treatment resulted in 7282 underexpressed genes in KO fibroblasts and 2567 overexpressed genes in KO fibroblasts (Figure 4A middle 3 lanes vs last 3 lanes, and Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—source data 2.

claim: The effect of sirolimus was less in WT cells with 2852 underexpressed genes and 223 overexpressed mRNAs.
source: The effect of sirolimus was less in WT cells with 2852 underexpressed genes and 223 overexpressed mRNAs (Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4—source data 3.

claim: Genes effected by sirolimus in WT fibroblasts were nearly a subset of the genes effected by sirolimus in KO fibroblasts.
source: Genes effected by sirolimus in WT fibroblasts were nearly a subset of the genes effected by sirolimus in KO fibroblasts (overexpressed genes 87% in common; underexpressed genes 88% in common).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of RNA sequencing data between WT and KO fibroblasts.

claim: Ninety-two percent (1275 of 1387) of genes overexpressed in KO compared to WT were also underexpressed after sirolimus treatment in KO.
source: Sirolimus corrected the effect of Tsc2-deficiency (WT vs. KO) for many mRNAs. Ninety-two percent (1275 of 1387) of genes overexpressed in KO compared to WT were also underexpressed after sirolimus treatment in KO.
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4—source data 4.

claim: Eighty percent (349 of 437) of genes that were underexpressed in KO versus WT were also overexpressed after sirolimus treatment in KO.
source: Likewise, 80% (349 of 437) of genes that were underexpressed in KO versus WT were also overexpressed after sirolimus treatment in KO (Figure 4—source data 4).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4—source data 4.

claim: Lgals3 was greater in KO than WT fibroblasts (p=0.007) and corrected by sirolimus.
source: Lgals3 was greater in KO than WT fibroblasts (p=0.007) and corrected by sirolimus (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Signature scores were greater in bladder tumors having non-silent TSC1 or TSC2 mutations versus other bladder tumors.
source: Signature scores were greater in tumors having non-silent TSC1 or TSC2 mutations versus other bladder tumors (Figure 4E) indicating that these cancers have an identifiable gene expression signature derived from inactivation of TSC1 or TSC2.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TSC1 and TSC2 mutant bladder tumors overexpressed LGALS3 versus other bladder tumors.
source: Interrogation of the TCGA cohort revealed that TSC1 and TSC2 mutant bladder tumors overexpressed LGALS3 versus other bladder tumors. (Figure 4F), suggesting that Gal-3 may be an individual marker for bladder cancers containing inactivating mutations in TSC1 or TSC2.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: In the forelimbs of WT mice, cells immunoreactive for Gal-3 were identified in larger vessels with staining seen in some skeletal muscle nuclei.
source: In the forelimbs of WT mice, cells immunoreactive for Gal-3 were identified in larger vessels with staining seen in some skeletal muscle nuclei (Figure 5A, left), whereas in the forelimb tumor of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice, areas of dense Gal-3 positivity were observed in both vascular and perivascular cells (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In the forelimb tumor of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice, areas of dense Gal-3 positivity were observed in both vascular and perivascular cells.
source: In the forelimbs of WT mice, cells immunoreactive for Gal-3 were identified in larger vessels with staining seen in some skeletal muscle nuclei (Figure 5A, left), whereas in the forelimb tumor of Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice, areas of dense Gal-3 positivity were observed in both vascular and perivascular cells (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Gal-3-positive cells were observed in both WT and Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice in the epidermis.
source: In the skin, Gal-3-positive cells were observed in both WT and Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice in the epidermis (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice contained increased numbers of Gal-3 positively stained dermal fibroblasts.
source: Additionally, Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice contained increased numbers of positively stained dermal fibroblasts (Figure 5B, lower).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: In early passage KO fibroblasts, both intracellular Gal-3 levels and secreted Gal-3 were sharply increased.
source: In early passage KO fibroblasts, both intracellular Gal-3 levels (Figure 5C) and secreted Gal-3 (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1) were sharply increased, and 48 hr sirolimus [20 nM] treatment resulted in their partial normalization.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and ELISA data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: 48 hr sirolimus treatment resulted in partial normalization of intracellular and secreted Gal-3 levels in KO fibroblasts.
source: In early passage KO fibroblasts, both intracellular Gal-3 levels (Figure 5C) and secreted Gal-3 (Figure 5D and Figure 5—source data 1) were sharply increased, and 48 hr sirolimus [20 nM] treatment resulted in their partial normalization.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and ELISA data shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: Serum of adult Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had 67% higher Gal-3 levels (p=0.015) than similar-age controls.
source: Serum of adult Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice had 67% higher Gal-3 levels (p=0.015) than similar-age controls (Figure 5E and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In sirolimus-treated Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice, Gal-3 serum levels were decreased by 25% (p=0.036).
source: In sirolimus-treated Tsc2cKOPrrx1-cre mice, Gal-3 serum levels were decreased by 25% (p=0.036) (Figure 5F and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Gal-3 immunostaining of normal-appearing control skin obtained from TSC patients showed positivity in the epidermis but very little in the dermis.
source: Gal-3 immunostaining of normal-appearing control skin obtained from TSC patients showed positivity in the epidermis but very little in the dermis (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: TSC skin tumors had abundant Gal-3 positive dermal fibroblasts.
source: In contrast, TSC skin tumors had abundant Gal-3 positive dermal fibroblasts (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Fibroblasts grown from TSC skin tumors released more Gal-3 than fibroblasts grown from normal-appearing skin.
source: Gal-3 ELISA of supernatants from fibroblasts grown from TSC skin tumors released more Gal-3 than fibroblasts grown from normal-appearing skin (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Western blot analysis demonstrated higher intracellular protein levels of Gal-3 in TSC skin tumor fibroblasts than paired normal-appearing skin fibroblasts.
source: Western blot analysis of samples from four patients demonstrated higher intracellular protein levels of Gal-3 in TSC skin tumor fibroblasts than paired normal-appearing skin fibroblasts, although absolute levels of Gal-3 varied among patients (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Gal-3 staining in tissue sections from lungs of patients with LAM showed Gal-3 expression in LAM nodules.
source: Gal-3 staining in tissue sections from lungs of patients with LAM showed Gal-3 expression in LAM nodules (LAM, Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In renal angiomyolipomas (AML), Gal-3 expression was observed in smooth muscle and adipose cells.
source: In renal angiomyolipomas (AML), Gal-3 expression was observed in smooth muscle and adipose cells (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: In patients with LAM not taking mTOR inhibitors, percent predicted one second forced expiratory volume (%FEV1) negatively correlated with Gal-3 levels.
source: In patients with LAM not taking mTOR inhibitors, percent predicted one second forced expiratory volume (%FEV1) negatively correlated with Gal-3 levels, (Figure 6G and Figure 6—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: In serum from patients that were being treated with mTOR inhibitors, no correlation of %FEV1 was found with Gal-3 serum levels.
source: In serum from patients that were being treated with mTOR inhibitors, no correlation of %FEV1 was found with Gal-3 serum levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Gal-3 levels were higher in the mild LAM group with AML compared to no AML suggesting AMLs were an additional source of serum Gal-3.
source: Gal-3 levels were also analyzed with two-way factorial ANOVA in treatment naïve patients with or without a confirmed diagnosis of AML, grouped according to severe LAM (%FEV1 <80) and mild LAM (%FEV1 >80). Gal-3 levels were higher in the mild LAM group with AML compared to no AML suggesting AMLs were an additional source of serum Gal-3 (Figure 6H- and Figure 6—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by ANOVA analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between BMI and galectin-3 in patients without mTOR inhibitor (r = 0.315, p=0.013).
source: There was a significant positive correlation between BMI and galectin-3 in patients without mTOR inhibitor (r = 0.315, p=0.013).
evidence: This is stated as a result of correlation analysis.

claim: After adjusting for BMI, the partial correlation coefficient between FEV1 and galectin-3 in patients without mTOR inhibitor was still significant (partial correlation r = −0.366, p=0.004).
source: After adjusting for BMI, the partial correlation coefficient between FEV1 and galectin-3 in patients without mTOR inhibitor was still significant (partial correlation r = −0.366, p=0.004).
evidence: This is stated as a result of partial correlation analysis.

claim: No significant difference in Gal-3 levels was observed between patients with LAM not taking mTOR inhibitor (4649 ± 1980 pg/mL, n = 64) and normal subjects (5023 ± 1646 pg/mL, n = 25).
source: No significant difference in Gal-3 levels was observed between patients with LAM not taking mTOR inhibitor (4649 ± 1980 pg/mL, n = 64) and normal subjects (5023 ± 1646 pg/mL, n = 25).
evidence: This is stated as a result of statistical comparison.

claim: Gal-3 may be an individual marker for bladder cancers containing inactivating mutations in TSC1 or TSC2.
source: Interrogation of the TCGA cohort revealed that TSC1 and TSC2 mutant bladder tumors overexpressed LGALS3 versus other bladder tumors. (Figure 4F), suggesting that Gal-3 may be an individual marker for bladder cancers containing inactivating mutations in TSC1 or TSC2.
evidence: This is suggested based on the observation that LGALS3 is overexpressed in TSC1/TSC2 mutant bladder tumors.

claim: Gal-3 is a pro-angiogenic lectin.
source: Gal-3, a pro-angiogenic lectin, was increased in mouse and human samples with TSC2 deficiency and Gal-3 serum levels correlated with LAM severity and the presence of AMLs in a cohort of patients with LAM.
evidence: This is stated as a known property of Gal-3.

claim: Analysis of human AMLs has demonstrated TSC2 loss and mTORC1 activation in vessel walls.
source: These models have demonstrated that Tsc1 deficiency in endothelial cells induces the formation of tumors by a mechanism involving mTORC1, but additional models are needed to replicate the pathological vascular changes observed in larger vessels in TSC, particularly since analysis of human AMLs has demonstrated TSC2 loss and mTORC1 activation in vessel walls (Karbowniczek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Karbowniczek et al., 2003.

claim: Prrx1-cre is expressed in the lateral plate mesoderm, which contains cells that give rise to the limb bud and craniofacial mesenchyme.
source: Here we report the generation of a mouse model with a Prrx1-cre transgene (Logan et al., 2002) to disrupt a conditional Tsc2 allele (Hernandez et al., 2007) in the lateral plate mesoderm, which contains cells that give rise to the limb bud and craniofacial mesenchyme.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Logan et al., 2002 and Hernandez et al., 2007.

claim: Galectin-3 is a lectin with specificity for beta-galactoside moieties on glycoproteins.
source: The only transcript that matched both lists in Figure 4B and C was Lgals3, which codes for galectin-3 (Gal-3), a lectin with specificity for beta-galactoside moieties on glycoproteins and has been reported to play roles in angiogenesis and fibrosis (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a known property of galectin-3 and supported by a citation to Li et al., 2014.

claim: Galectin-3 has been reported to play roles in angiogenesis and fibrosis.
source: The only transcript that matched both lists in Figure 4B and C was Lgals3, which codes for galectin-3 (Gal-3), a lectin with specificity for beta-galactoside moieties on glycoproteins and has been reported to play roles in angiogenesis and fibrosis (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2014.
